messages.content: help me understand to, too, and two with simple examples.
to can show where you go: i went to the library. too can mean also: my sister came too. two is a number: we read two books.
can too mean something other than also?
yes. too can say there is more of something than works for a need. this cup is too small says the size is a problem for what you want.
use two and too in one sentence.
two people cannot sit here because the space is too small.
now use all three in a short story.
i went to the library with two friends. my sister wanted to come too.
what if i write i went two the library?
use to there. you are talking about the place you went, not the number two.
now just give one sentence about two books.
i read two books.
make it a sentence where my brother read them as well.
i read two books, and my brother read them too.
does too tell us he read the same books?
in that sentence, them is about the two books you read, so yes. too says he did the reading as well.
my holiday was quiet. i read, cooked, and visited my aunt once. when people ask what i did, i feel like i need a longer answer.
you can give the real answer without making the holiday sound busy. those are things you did, even if there was no long journey.
can you help me say it in one sentence?
i had a quiet holiday with time to read, cook, and visit my aunt.
would quiet make it sound like i did not enjoy it?
not by itself. quiet gives an idea of the kind of time you had, not whether it was good or wrong for you.
i did enjoy it. add that without saying no other holiday could be better.
i enjoyed a quiet holiday with time to read, cook, and visit my aunt.
what if someone asks why i did not go away?
you can say you chose to stay near home if that is true, or give another real reason you want to share. you do not have to make up a journey to make the holiday sound useful.
make that explanation shorter.
you can tell the real reason or keep the answer short. you do not need a made up journey.
only give the sentence about what i enjoyed again.
i enjoyed a quiet holiday with time to read, cook, and visit my aunt.
write a story about a child who is asked to follow a line on paper and then learns it is not the line for his task.

a child sat with a page that had a road drawing and a story on it. his teacher asked him to follow the line with his hand. he put his hand on the road and moved it slowly across the page. she wanted him to follow the first line of the story. when she saw what he was doing, she stopped and explained which line she wanted. he showed her the two choices and asked her to say the story line next time. she said thank you for helping her see why the request had not been clear. the word line had worked for both parts of the page, so they needed more detail to choose one.
why did he choose the road?
it was a line he could see on the page. the teacher had not said that she wanted him to follow the words of the story.
was he wrong about the road being a line?
no. the problem was choosing which line the request was about.
write a more clear request from the teacher.
please follow the first line of the story with your hand as we read it.
make that request shorter.
please follow the first line of the story with your hand.
what changed when she explained?
the child knew which part of the page she wanted him to follow.
finish with him at the words, without another explanation.
he put his hand under the first sentence and moved it along while she read.
an animal is near my door. can you know whether it wants to come inside?
no. being near the door does not by itself tell us what the animal wants.
what if i say it keeps looking at the door?
that gives more about what it is doing, but it still does not tell us for sure why it is looking. there may be different reasons.
make that explanation shorter.
it gives where the animal is looking, but not for sure why.
can you know it is hungry?
not from those facts. you have not given information about whether it is hungry or has had food.
i say it has just had food and is now sleeping. what changes?
now you have given that it had food and is sleeping. i can use those facts without saying i know every need or feeling it has.
make that answer shorter.
i can use the facts you gave without saying i know every need or feeling it has.
what question could i answer to give you more about the place?
you could say whether the door is open or closed, and whether the animal is inside or outside.
it is outside and the door is closed. only give those details back.
the animal is outside, near a closed door.
i have three pages on my desk. two have the same sentence and one has a different sentence. how many different sentences are there?
there are two different sentences.
how many pages have writing?
all three pages have writing.
now i add a new page with one of the same sentences on it.
then four pages have writing, but there are still two different sentences.
why did the new page not make a new sentence?
because you wrote a sentence already in the group. a new page can hold the same words as another page.
now i change the sentence on only the new page to something different from both old sentences.
then there are three different sentences across the four pages.
can you know which words changed?
no. you said the sentence changed, but did not give the old or new words.
only give how many pages there are.
four pages.
now only how many different sentences.
three different sentences.
i want to ask my friend if a book is short. i am not asking whether it is easy. how do i say that?
you could ask: about how many pages does the book have?
can i simply say is it short?
yes, but people may use short in a general way. asking about pages gives a more specific idea of how much reading there is.
make that explanation shorter.
a page number gives a more specific answer than just short or long.
what if the pages have very small writing?
then the number of pages may not tell the whole story about reading time. you can also ask whether the writing is small or whether each page has many words.
write two simple questions for that.
about how many pages does it have? are there many words on each page?
why not ask is it a good book instead?
is it a good book asks what your friend thinks of the book. it does not ask how much reading there is.
explain that more simply.
is it a good book asks what your friend thinks of the book. it does not ask how long it is.
only give the pages question again.
about how many pages does it have?
write a story about a family making a note for someone who has never visited their house. they should not use left or right until the starting place is clear.

a family wanted a friend to find the room where they would have dinner. the son wrote turn left and come in. his mother asked where the friend would be standing when reading that. from the front door, left went to the kitchen. from the garden door, left went to the bedroom. they added start at the front door before the rest of the message. then they gave the room name too, so the friend could ask if something was still not clear. the note did not become much longer, but it now had a place to begin.
why was left not enough?
left can be a different choice from a different starting place. the front door and garden door did not give the same way to the kitchen.
explain using each starting place.
turning left from the front door went to the kitchen. turning left from the garden door went to the bedroom.
write the useful note.
start at the front door. turn left to the kitchen, where we will have dinner.
can the same note work if the friend comes through the garden door?
not without giving a way to reach the front door first or giving another way from the garden door.
what question could the friend ask if they are at the garden door?
i am at the garden door. which way should i go from here?
finish with them reading the note from the front door to check it.
they stood at the front door and used the words to go to the kitchen. the son made sure the first line gave the starting place clearly.
i can read a simple story, but i still ask many questions about grammar. sometimes that makes me think i do not know anything.
asking grammar questions does not take away the reading you can already do. you can understand a story and still want to know why a sentence works.
can understanding the story and understanding grammar be different?
yes. you can know what a story says without knowing how to explain every sentence in it. those are not the same task.
make that answer shorter.
you can know what a story says without knowing how to explain every sentence in it.
help me say what i can do without saying i know all the grammar.
i can read simple stories, and i am still learning how the grammar works.
what if someone says then you cannot read?
you can give a specific example of what you do understand. you do not have to choose between knowing everything and knowing nothing.
make that into a short reply.
i can understand a simple story even when i still have questions about some sentences.
now only give the sentence about learning.
i can read simple stories, and i am still learning how the grammar works.
